body_markdown:
Driving older cars involves a certain amount of risk. Newer cars are, of course, designed and built to minimize such risk, as they have redundant systems and monitors that will typically give warning well before actual failures occur. Old cars may have similar warnings, but usually they come when action is required *now,* instead of on an “investigate when convenient” timeline.


If you’re the sort of vintage car owner who pops the hood and has already formulated a repair plan before your hood ornament reaches maximum elevation, the following list may seem a tad basic. But if you’re more the type of owner whose focus is on enjoying the drive and leaving the wrenching to your favorite mechanic, the idea of making your own on-the-road repairs can be scary.


We’re here to suggest that it doesn’t have to be that way. With some advance vigilance, the nightmare of an imminent breakdown shouldn’t be something that keeps you up at night, draining the joy out of tomorrow’s Sunday drive.


## First, remain calm


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Take your vintage vehicle on enough drives, for enough miles, and the concept of getting stuck on the side of the road is not *if,* but *when.* Yes, being stranded is inconvenient at best, frightening at worst, but you can dilute both those extremes, and everything in between, with the aforementioned proper planning. Even in the worst case, panic and drama won’t help. Maintaining a level head and enacting your plan to move forward (pun intended) will help your own mental state, and certainly tamp down your passengers’ concerns. This is a good time to take that obligatory deep breath and begin to consider your options.


## Know how to get help


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Do you have a plan to get help, or are you the sort of person who figures it out on the fly? Most of us have been the latter, and the experience forced us to become the former. We are blessed to be living in the era of the (charged up) cell phone, and it has changed everything. For an around-town trip, your disaster plan might include phoning a friend, or having a preferred tow service on speed-dial. If you have a roadside assistance plan or[club membership](https://www.hagerty.com/drivers-club/marketing/roadside) , that number should also be on your phone’s contact list. But even if your plan is to just get the tools out of the trunk, it’s smart to mentally play through some trouble scenarios in advance. You need to consider contingency plans for issues like, for example, the lack of cell signal, or a problem that’s too big to handle on the side of the road.


## Carry the right tools, even if you can’t use them


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Even if you aren’t mentally or physically prepared to make a repair, that doesn’t mean someone who stops to help you won’t be. Having[a few tools in the trunk](https://www.hagerty.com/media/hagerty-community/according-to-you-essential-tools-for-a-road-trip-tool-kit/) can mean the difference between a tow and driving home with a mere delay. I once helped a friend change an alternator in a parking lot, and it was only possible because they already had tools aboard. I was away from home and had no access to my own, but I did have the time to swing by and help get the work done.


Put some extra consideration into tools that might be unique or special for your car. The 1965 Chevrolet Corvair I love to drive requires a special 9/16-inch wrench with a little bend in it that makes changing or installing a fan belt a lot easier than just using a standard wrench. Of course, I keep a new belt tucked right next to the wrench. Effective preparation makes the thought of breaking down a lot less frightening.


## Get creative if needed


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Being stuck on the side of the road gives you all the time in the world to think. Don’t waste that opportunity; use it to help force your brain to figure out a solution to your problem. A hairpin used to hold a shift linkage together; a hunk of rubber found in a ditch applied to a carburetor problem; using a length of speaker wire to bypass a section of wiring for the ignition system that got too close to the hot exhaust—those were all spur-of-the-moment repairs that got me home.


Anyone with a lot of miles in older cars will have stories of creative repairs. If you only have a few miles on your classic, be aware that sooner rather than later, you will likely have a story or two of your own. Sometimes reading about them is[a fun way to study up](https://www.hagerty.com/media/hagerty-community/according-to-you-whats-your-best-roadside-repair-story/) and learn just how creative you can get.


Is this modest listicle going to take all the stress out of driving an old car? Hardly. But hopefully these items can help keep driving your vintage vehicle fun, rather than be the source of cautionary nightmares. If you have a story about how you prepare for a future potential breakdown, or a trick roadside repair you made, please leave it as a comment below. You never know who you might help…
